title: Managing Panic - Yours and Others'
summary: How to notice the panic response early, bring yourself back with slow breathing and grounding, and calm a frightened person or group by giving them something to do.

steps.title: Recognize the signs early
steps.body: Fear is a normal reaction to danger. It can make you careful, or it can freeze you. Military survival training calls panic one of the biggest threats in any survival situation because it wrecks judgment. Learn your own early signs: pounding heart, fast shallow breathing, tunnel vision, shaking hands, a dry mouth, and an urge to run or do something - anything - right now. The thinking part of your brain works worse when this happens. Name it to yourself as soon as you notice it: 'This is adrenaline. I need 60 seconds to get my head back.' Naming the reaction does not make it go away, but it reminds you not to make a big decision in the first rush of fear. Unless there is an immediate threat like fire or a collapse, a short pause is almost always safe.

steps.title: Slow your breathing
steps.body: Slow breathing is one of the simplest tools the VA National Center for PTSD recommends for staying calm. One easy pattern is box breathing: breathe in through your nose for a count of 4, hold for 4, breathe out slowly through your mouth for 4, hold for 4. Repeat 4 to 6 times. If holding your breath feels bad, just make each breath out longer than the breath in - for example, in for 4 and out for 6. Drop your shoulders and unclench your jaw while you do it. You should notice your heart rate easing and your thinking getting clearer within a minute or two. Practice this daily when you are calm, a few minutes at a time. A skill practiced in calm times is much easier to use when you are scared.

steps.title: Ground yourself in the present
steps.body: When your mind is racing through worst-case scenarios, pull your attention back to what is real right now. The 5-4-3-2-1 method works well: name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, and 1 you can taste. Say them out loud or under your breath, and be specific ('the green flashlight, the wet floor'). Press your feet into the ground and your hands onto a solid surface. The VA recommends focusing on your breathing or your senses in this way to feel safer after a disaster. Once you feel steadier, pick one small, concrete next action - check the water jug, look out the window, count supplies. Action is the bridge back to clear thinking.

steps.title: Calm yourself before you calm others
steps.body: Fear spreads through a group, and so does calm. If you try to settle someone while you are still panicked, you will usually make it worse. Take three slow breaths first. Then lower your voice, slow your speech, and use short sentences. Get to their eye level. Say their name. Try: 'Sam, look at me. You're safe right now. Breathe with me.' Then breathe slowly together where they can see you. Ask before touching; a hand on the shoulder helps some people and scares others. Do not say 'calm down' - it is not an instruction anyone can follow. Do not lie ('everything is fine') when it is clearly not; false reassurance destroys trust the moment reality shows up.

steps.title: Give them a job
steps.body: A panicking person needs something to focus on that is not the threat. Once they can hear you, give one simple, useful task with a clear end: 'Hold this light on the door,' 'Fill these two bottles,' 'Count how many cans we have.' A real job gives the mind something to grip and helps restore a sense of control. Check back in a few minutes and thank them for doing it. Keep tasks short and easy at first, and step up to bigger jobs as they settle. Children respond well to this too - give them real, safe work, not pretend tasks.

steps.title: Stop group panic from spreading
steps.body: When several people start to panic at once, speak to the whole group in a firm, level voice: 'Everyone stop. Listen. Here is what we are doing right now.' Then give one clear plan and assign people by name. If one person is spiraling, move them a few steps away from the group with one calm helper so the fear does not spread. In a true emergency - fire, gas smell, collapse - the plan is simply to move to safety; skip the calming and lead the way out. Watch the group for the next 10 to 15 minutes, because fear often comes back in waves as new information arrives.

steps.title: Talk it through afterward
steps.body: When the danger has passed, take a few minutes to talk about what happened without blame. Panic is a body reaction, not a weakness. Ask: What set it off? What were the first signs? What helped? What would we do differently? Write down what worked so the group can use it next time. Normal reactions after a scary event include trouble sleeping, irritability, and replaying the event. These often fade over days to weeks. If someone keeps having panic attacks, cannot function, or talks about harming themselves, get professional help as soon as you can. In the U.S., call or text 988 for the crisis line, or call or text the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990.

warnings: Chest pain, fainting, trouble breathing, or confusion can be a heart attack, asthma, low blood sugar, or other medical emergency, not panic. Treat it as medical until you are sure, and call 911 if you can.
Do not make big, permanent decisions in the first rush of fear unless staying put is clearly deadly.
Do not physically restrain a panicking person unless they are about to hurt themselves or someone else. Restraint usually makes panic worse.
False reassurance ('help is on the way') that turns out wrong costs you the group's trust when you need it most.
proTips: Practice slow breathing for 2-5 minutes a day so it becomes automatic before you ever need it.
Agree on a family 'panic plan' ahead of time: who calms whom, what words you will use, and what simple job each person takes.
Keep small, concrete tasks ready to hand out - filling water, counting supplies, holding a light - so you never have to think one up under stress.
Your face and voice set the tone. Take one slow breath before you speak to the group.
source: U.S. Marine Corps survival training (FM 21-76) / VA National Center for PTSD / SAMHSA

sources.title: RP0401 Field Survival (based on FM 21-76 / MCRP 3-02F Survival)
sources.publisher: U.S. Marine Corps Training and Education Command

sources.title: How to Cope With Traumatic Events and Disasters

whenNotTo: When there is an immediate physical danger (fire, gas, collapse, rising water) - move people to safety first and calm them afterward.
When the person may be having a medical emergency such as a heart attack, asthma attack, or diabetic low - treat the medical problem first.

quickGlance.situation: You or someone near you is starting to panic during an emergency.
immediate: Move away from any immediate physical danger first.
Breathe slowly: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4 - repeat 4 to 6 times.
Speak low and slow, use the person's name, and breathe with them.
Give them one simple, real task to do.
then: Watch the group for the next 10-15 minutes for fear coming back.
Talk it through later and note what worked.
Get professional help if panic keeps returning; call or text 988 in a crisis.

title: Decision Making Under Stress
summary: Simple, repeatable ways to make good-enough decisions fast when stress, fatigue, and missing information make clear thinking hard.

steps.title: Know what stress does to your thinking
steps.body: Under stress, people jump to fast, gut-level choices and stop weighing options. That works when the situation is familiar. It fails when the problem is new or has trade-offs - which describes most emergencies. Stress also narrows attention, so you fixate on the loudest problem and miss quieter, deadlier ones. You will not out-think this in the moment. Instead, carry a few simple decision habits that you have practiced ahead of time, so they kick in automatically. The U.S. military survival acronym SURVIVAL starts with 'Size up the situation' and 'Use all your senses; haste wastes' for this reason: a short, deliberate look beats a fast wrong move.

steps.title: Size up before you act
steps.body: Take 30 to 60 seconds to look, listen, and count. Ask three questions: What is happening right now? What is about to get worse? What do we have to work with - people, tools, water, time? CERT leadership training uses a similar process: define all the problems, look at the information carefully, pick out the problems your team can actually handle, rank them, and choose a course of action for each. Say what you know and what you do not know out loud, even if only to yourself. If you are leading, share it with the group. Separating facts ('the water is at the second step') from guesses ('the road is probably out') keeps rumors from steering the decision.

steps.title: Put problems in the right order
steps.body: When several things are wrong at once, handle them in this order. First, threats to life right now: fire, severe bleeding, gas, rising water, extreme cold or heat. Second, problems that are stable but will get much worse soon: a small leak, a dropping fuel supply, a person getting sicker. Third, basic needs: safe water, shelter, warmth, food, sanitation, communication. Fourth, everything that makes life easier. People often skip to the fourth group because it feels productive. Reorganizing supplies while a heater is filling the room with carbon monoxide is a classic mistake. Write the list down and work it top to bottom.

steps.title: Use a fast loop: observe, orient, decide, act
steps.body: The OODA loop, developed by U.S. Air Force Colonel John Boyd, is a handy way to keep moving. Observe: what is actually happening? Orient: what does it mean, given what you know? Decide: pick one course of action. Act: do it. Then go straight back to Observe and check whether it worked. The point is not one perfect decision but many small, correctable ones. Make the decision, watch the result, and adjust. If the first plan is not working, CERT training says to switch to your backup plan rather than pushing harder on a failing one.

steps.title: Accept a good-enough answer on a deadline
steps.body: Waiting for perfect information is itself a decision, and often a bad one. Set a time limit that fits the stakes: seconds for a fire, minutes for whether to evacuate, hours for a supply plan. When the time is up, choose the best option you have. Many military leaders use a rough '70 percent' rule - if you have most of the information and more waiting will cost you, decide. Then tell people the plan clearly and say when you will re-check it ('We stay put; I'll reassess at noon'). A scheduled re-check makes it easier to commit now without feeling locked in.

steps.title: Fight decision fatigue
steps.body: Every decision uses up a little of your mental energy, and the quality of decisions drops as the hours and the decisions pile up, especially without sleep or food. Make routine choices ahead of time with simple rules: 'If the power is out more than 4 hours, we move the freezer food to coolers.' Rules turn decisions into actions. Hand routine decisions to other people. Save the big, hard-to-reverse choices for times when you have eaten and rested. If you have been awake a long time, say so and ask someone else to double-check your thinking.

steps.title: Check your blind spots
steps.body: Stress makes everyone seek information that agrees with what they already think. Before a major decision, ask one person to argue against it, or run a quick 'pre-mortem': imagine the plan failed, and list the most likely reasons. Fix the top one or two. Write the decision and the reason on paper in one sentence. Writing forces you to be precise, helps the next shift understand what was decided, and prevents arguments later about who said what.

warnings: Analysis paralysis - circling options without choosing - can be as dangerous as a poor choice. Set a deadline and keep it.
Fatigue and hunger quietly wreck judgment. Do not make irreversible decisions while badly sleep-deprived if they can wait.
Rumors spread fast in a crisis. Act on verified information from official alerts, your own eyes, or trusted reports.
proTips: Keep a small notebook for decisions: time, decision, reason, re-check time.
Write 'if-then' rules for your most likely emergencies now, while you are calm.
Ask 'What will this look like in an hour if we do nothing?' to spot problems that are about to get worse.
source: U.S. Marine Corps survival training (FM 21-76) / FEMA CERT

sources.title: RP0401 Field Survival (based on FM 21-76 / MCRP 3-02F Survival)
sources.publisher: U.S. Marine Corps Training and Education Command

sources.title: IS-100.c Introduction to the Incident Command System (class handouts)
sources.publisher: FEMA Emergency Management Institute (via URMC Finger Lakes Regional Training Center)

whenNotTo: When a trained responder (firefighter, police, EMS) is on scene and giving instructions - follow them.
When an official evacuation order is in place - leave; do not re-decide it.

quickGlance.situation: You must decide something important fast while stressed and missing information.
immediate: Take 30-60 seconds to size up: what is happening, what will get worse, what do we have?
Handle life threats first, then problems about to get worse, then basic needs.
Set a decision deadline and pick the best option when it arrives.
then: Announce the plan and when you will re-check it.
Ask someone to argue against big decisions before you commit.
Write down the decision and the reason.

title: Group Leadership in a Crisis
summary: How to step up and lead a household, neighbors, or a group of strangers in an emergency: earn trust fast, give clear assignments, match your style to the situation, and hand off leadership before you burn out.

steps.title: Earn authority by being calm and useful
steps.body: In a crisis, people follow whoever seems to know what to do, not whoever has the biggest title. Earn that trust in the first few minutes. Take a short, visible look around. Then say plainly what you know and what you do not: 'The power is out across the whole street. I don't know for how long yet.' Then take one useful action on the biggest problem. Honesty about what you don't know builds trust; false certainty destroys it the moment reality disagrees. If someone in the group clearly has more relevant skill - a nurse for an injury, an electrician for a downed line - let them lead that part. Good leaders know when to step aside.

steps.title: Give a short first briefing
steps.body: Within the first few minutes, gather people and give a briefing of about one minute. Cover four things: what happened, what we know and don't know, what we are doing right now, and who is doing what. Assign tasks by name, with a time to report back: 'Maria, check on everyone in the back rooms and tell me in 10 minutes. Dev, find every flashlight and bring them here. Lee, stay with me.' Use plain words, short sentences, and ask people to repeat key instructions back. CERT leadership training stresses these same habits: clear, simple directions and confirming people understood.

steps.title: Find out what people can do
steps.body: Ask the group directly: 'Who has medical training? Who knows this building or area? Who has a vehicle, a radio, tools?' Match jobs to real skills and to people's physical limits. Military survival training emphasizes assigning tasks according to each person's abilities and looking after one another. Keep the span of control small: the Incident Command System suggests one supervisor for about five people. If you have more than that, name a few small-team leads and talk mainly to them. Pair people up so no one works alone on risky tasks. Keep a simple list of who is doing what so jobs don't fall through the cracks.

steps.title: Match your style to the situation
steps.body: CERT training describes three leadership styles. When lives are in immediate danger, be directive: take input quickly, but decide and give clear orders. When the situation is controlled but still serious, be participative: ask for ideas, then decide. When there is a settled plan and no immediate danger, be delegative: let team members make decisions within their jobs, while you stay informed and available. A useful test: How bad is a wrong decision, and how much time do we have? High stakes and little time call for command. Lower stakes and more time call for discussion. Using command for everything breeds resentment; using a vote during a fire gets people hurt.

steps.title: Handle disagreement quickly and fairly
steps.body: Conflict in a stressed group is normal. Deal with it early, before it festers. In urgent moments, give each side one short hearing, decide, explain why in one sentence, and move on. Disagreement is allowed; refusing to cooperate on safety is not. Revisit a decision only when new facts appear, not because someone keeps pushing. For longer-running conflicts over chores, space, or supplies, use the step-by-step approach in the conflict guide (psych-006). If a dispute turns threatening, focus on calming it and keeping people safe (see sec-009).

steps.title: Look after your people and yourself
steps.body: A team runs on rest, food, and water. Brief people before each task, rotate hard or risky jobs, and enforce breaks away from the scene. Watch for signs of strain: irritability, mistakes, withdrawal, or someone pushing far past exhaustion. Leaders burn out fastest because they never stop. Name a second-in-charge early. When you need rest, hand over with a short briefing - what is happening, what is in progress, what is planned - just as ICS requires a briefing at every change of command. CERT leadership training also suggests that if a leader is clearly worn out, one or two members should quietly ask whether they need help.

steps.title: Shift to shared leadership for the long haul
steps.body: One-person command works for the first hours. Over days or weeks it causes burnout, resentment, and a dangerous single point of failure. Once things stabilize, spread out responsibility: one person owns water and food, one owns medical and hygiene, one owns communications, one owns safety and night watch. Hold a short daily meeting to set priorities together. Write down shared rules, especially for supplies (see psych-009). Do a short after-action talk after big events: what worked, what didn't, what we change. Keep it under 30 minutes and focused on fixes, not blame.

warnings: Losing your temper or visibly panicking in front of the group can cost you its trust for the rest of the event.
Pure top-down command for days on end shuts down initiative - people stop reporting problems you cannot see yourself.
Never send someone alone to do a risky task. Use pairs and set a check-in time.
proTips: Assign by name. 'Someone check the back door' means no one will.
Decide ahead of time who leads in which emergency at home - fire, medical, security - so there is no argument when it happens.
Ask people to repeat instructions back. It catches misunderstandings in seconds.
Free FEMA training (IS-100.c for ICS, IS-317 for CERT) is a low-cost way to build real leadership skills before a disaster.
source: FEMA CERT / FEMA ICS-100 / U.S. Marine Corps survival training (FM 21-76)

sources.title: IS-100.c Introduction to the Incident Command System (class handouts)
sources.publisher: FEMA Emergency Management Institute (via URMC Finger Lakes Regional Training Center)

sources.title: RP0401 Field Survival (based on FM 21-76 / MCRP 3-02F Survival)
sources.publisher: U.S. Marine Corps Training and Education Command

whenNotTo: When police, fire, or EMS are on scene - support their instructions instead of running a parallel operation.
When someone else is already leading well - back them up rather than competing for control.

quickGlance.situation: A group is looking for direction in an emergency and no one is leading.
immediate: Look around briefly, then say what you know and don't know.
Give a one-minute briefing and assign tasks by name with report-back times.
Ask who has medical skills, tools, or local knowledge.
then: Keep small teams of about five with a lead each.
Name a second-in-charge and rotate rest.
Spread responsibilities once things stabilize.

title: Morale and Psychological Endurance
summary: How to keep yourself and your group going through a long emergency: honest hope, daily routine, small wins, connection, and room for grief.

steps.title: Expect the slump after the first few days
steps.body: In the first hours of a disaster, adrenaline and urgency carry most people. After a few days that energy fades. Exhaustion builds, the length of the situation sinks in, and feelings pushed aside earlier come back. Military survival training lists the common stressors: injury or illness, uncertainty and lack of control, the environment, hunger and thirst, fatigue, and isolation. Their effects pile up. Plan for this slump. Around day two or three, hold a short group talk to say out loud that you are moving from 'getting through tonight' to 'living like this for a while,' reset expectations, and ask how people are holding up.

steps.title: Build hope on a plan, not a promise
steps.body: Real hope has two parts: believing things can improve, and knowing what you can do to help them improve. Hope built on a rescue date you can't confirm collapses when the date passes. Give the group facts and actions instead: 'I don't know when power comes back. Here's what I do know: we have water for 9 days, the radio works, and today we're going to fix the rain catch.' Avoid both extremes. 'Everything will be fine' sounds dismissive and erodes trust. 'We're done for' drains the energy people need to act. Honest difficulty, plus real strengths, plus a next step, is the formula.

steps.title: Create a daily routine
steps.body: Uncertainty feeds anxiety. Routine gives the brain something predictable to hold onto. Set fixed wake and sleep times, regular meals even if small, and a short morning briefing (5 to 10 minutes: status, today's priorities, who does what). Add an evening check-in. Give everyone a real job each day, including children and older adults, matched to what they can safely do. Protect rest periods - don't just schedule them, enforce them. The VA National Center for PTSD recommends setting simple daily goals and breaking big problems into small steps to rebuild a sense of control after a disaster.

steps.title: Find and name small wins
steps.body: Big problems - weeks without power, unclear rescue, shrinking supplies - feel paralyzing because the gap is so large. Break them into daily goals the group can actually finish: 'Today we inventory all the food.' 'Today we check on the neighbors at number 12.' When a goal is met, say so out loud: 'We collected 5 gallons of rainwater today. That's two more days of drinking water. Good work.' Keep a visible tally on paper or a whiteboard. Each finished goal is proof that effort pays off, which keeps people working. The VA also recommends celebrating small successes as part of recovering from disaster.

steps.title: Keep people connected
steps.body: Isolation is one of the main survival stressors. Social support is one of the strongest protections against lasting distress. Eat together when you can. Check on people who go quiet. Link up with neighbors, especially those who live alone, are older, or have disabilities. Helping others also lifts the helper's mood. Limit how much disaster news people take in, especially right before sleep - get updates at set times, then turn it off. Small comforts on a schedule, like a hot drink, a card game, music, or a story at night, do more for morale than their cost suggests.

steps.title: Make room for grief and anger
steps.body: People may be grieving lost homes, pets, routines, health, or people. Grief that is ignored often shows up as anger, withdrawal, risky behavior, or conflict. Name losses openly and kindly: 'Marcus hasn't heard from his family in two days. That's hard.' Offer a short, optional time each evening where people can talk or just sit. Simple rituals - writing about a loss, a moment of silence - help. Anger and irritability are common after disasters; exercise, journaling, and taking a break before a tense conversation all help. Then return to the next small task. Acknowledge, allow, and move forward.

steps.title: Know when someone needs more help
steps.body: Most people bounce back over time, and there is no single right way to cope. Get professional help as soon as you can if someone cannot function for days, stops eating or drinking, uses alcohol or drugs heavily, talks about hopelessness or harming themselves, or seems out of touch with reality. In the U.S., call or text 988 (Veterans press 1). The SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 offers free crisis counseling by call or text. Do not leave someone who talks about suicide alone; remove obvious means of harm if it is safe to do so and get help. Psychological first aid basics are in health-013.

warnings: Treat morale collapse as a real threat: it leads to poor decisions, conflict, and people splitting off from the group.
Never mock someone's emotional reaction. What looks like overreaction is often many stresses hitting at once.
Talk of suicide or self-harm is an emergency. Stay with the person and get help - call or text 988.
proTips: Schedule small pleasures - coffee at 7, cards at 8 - so people have something to look forward to.
Humor helps when it is kind and earned. Never aim it at someone's fear or loss.
True survival stories (polar expeditions, shipwrecks) remind people that humans endure far worse.
Give children real, safe jobs; feeling useful lowers their anxiety and the adults' too.
source: VA National Center for PTSD / SAMHSA / U.S. Marine Corps survival training (FM 21-76)

sources.title: How to Cope With Traumatic Events and Disasters
RP0401 Field Survival (based on FM 21-76 / MCRP 3-02F Survival)
sources.publisher: U.S. Marine Corps Training and Education Command

whenNotTo: These are group-morale and self-care tools, not treatment. Someone who is suicidal, severely depressed, or out of touch with reality needs professional help.

quickGlance.situation: Your group is days into an emergency and energy, hope, or patience is running low.
immediate: Hold a short talk to reset expectations and ask how people are doing.
Set a daily routine with a morning briefing and an evening check-in.
Pick one small goal for today and celebrate it when it is done.
then: Make time each evening to acknowledge losses.
Check on quiet or isolated people, including neighbors.
Get help for anyone who cannot function or talks about self-harm - call or text 988.

title: Sleep Deprivation Management
summary: How to keep a household or group safe when no one is getting enough sleep: know the impairment, rotate rest, nap smart, use caffeine carefully, and keep tired people away from dangerous jobs.

steps.title: Understand how impaired tired people are
steps.body: CDC's NIOSH notes that being awake for 17 hours affects performance about as much as a blood alcohol level of 0.05 percent, and 24 hours awake is similar to 0.10 percent - above the 0.08 percent legal driving limit in the U.S. Tired people react slower, make more mistakes, lose their temper faster, and communicate poorly. The worst part: sleep-deprived people are bad at judging their own impairment. Someone who has been up all night may honestly believe they are fine. Do not rely on 'I'm okay' from a tired person. Use hours awake and visible signs to decide who does what.

steps.title: Watch for the warning signs
steps.body: NIOSH lists yawning, trouble concentrating, emotional swings, flawed logic, and poor communication as signs of fatigue. Also watch for heavy or slow blinking, a glassy stare, head nodding then jerking up, trailing off mid-sentence, and forgetting what was just said. These can come before microsleeps - brief lapses of a few seconds that the person often doesn't notice. A microsleep while driving, cooking over a flame, or on watch can be deadly. If you see these signs in yourself, stop the risky task. If you see them in someone else, relieve them now. Use a buddy system: pair people up to keep an eye on each other's fatigue.

steps.title: Never let everyone sleep at once - and never let one person carry it all
steps.body: In an extended emergency, set up a rest and watch rotation. With 4 adults and 2-hour watches, each person can get about 6 hours of sleep in an 8-hour night. With fewer people, use shorter watches or accept a watch that only covers the riskiest hours. Keep watch duty simple and active: listen, do quick checks at irregular times, write down anything unusual, and know how to wake everyone fast. At each handover, give a short verbal briefing of anything seen or heard. See sec-012 for setting up a night watch. NIOSH advises at least 10 hours off in each 24 hours for workers on long shifts and avoiding shifts over 12 hours when you can.

steps.title: Decide who sleeps first
steps.body: When sleep is short, don't share it out at random. The main decision-maker should get protected sleep, because tired judgment at the top affects everyone. People doing medical care, driving, or other dangerous work come next. Then rotate everyone else. Make sleep as good as possible: dark, quiet, cool, and with earplugs or an eye mask if you have them. Keep a short, consistent routine before sleep. Avoid alcohol and nicotine for 2 to 3 hours before sleeping, and limit bright screens for about an hour and a half before bed - both NIOSH recommendations.

steps.title: Nap on purpose
steps.body: Naps help but do not replace real sleep. NIOSH recommends short naps of 15 to 30 minutes to reduce fatigue during a long shift; set an alarm. Longer naps of about 1.5 hours can help before a night of work when hours are very long. The easiest times to nap are early morning, mid-afternoon, and during the night. Expect grogginess right after waking, called sleep inertia. Allow time for it to pass before doing anything critical. Bright light, washing your face, or a small amount of caffeine helps. One trick: drink a cup of coffee right before a short nap - caffeine takes about 30 minutes to kick in, so it starts working as you wake.

steps.title: Use caffeine as a tool, not a fix
steps.body: Caffeine makes you feel more alert but does not undo sleep loss. It can make a tired person feel fine while still making mistakes. Use it at the times you most need to be sharp, not all day. NIOSH notes that about 100 mg (roughly one 5-ounce cup of brewed coffee) can help shake off post-nap grogginess, and suggests stopping caffeine about 5 hours before you plan to sleep. Heavy daily use builds tolerance, so it works less. Be careful with energy drinks and caffeine pills; too much caffeine can affect the heart and nervous system. If you cut back, do it gradually to avoid headaches and irritability, and drink extra water.

steps.title: Plan the recovery
steps.body: After days of short sleep, one long night helps a lot but usually doesn't fully restore you. Plan for at least two good nights. Mood and patience are often the last to recover, so expect irritability and short tempers for a day or two after. Lower the bar for conflict during that time and give people space. Avoid big, permanent decisions until people have had real sleep. If someone cannot sleep for many nights even when they have the chance, or has ongoing nightmares, panic, or confusion, they may need medical or mental-health help.

warnings: Do not let a badly sleep-deprived person drive, run a stove or heater, give medical care, or stand watch alone.
The most dangerous tired person is the one who insists they are fine. Go by hours awake and visible signs.
Willpower does not stop microsleeps. If warning signs appear, the only fixes are sleep or removing the person from the risky task.
Too much caffeine, especially from energy drinks or pills, can cause heart rhythm problems. Follow product labels.
proTips: Write the watch and rest schedule on paper and post it so no one has to remember or argue about it.
A cup of coffee just before a 15-20 minute nap helps you wake up sharper.
Bright light at the start of a night watch helps alertness; keep sleeping areas as dark as possible.
Use a buddy system so everyone has someone checking them for fatigue.

sources.title: Impairments due to sleep deprivation are similar to impairments due to alcohol intoxication (Work Schedules training, Module 3)
Managing Fatigue During Times of Crisis: Guidance for Nurses, Managers, and Other Healthcare Workers

whenNotTo: Do not use caffeine or naps to keep driving when drowsy if you can safely stop and sleep instead.
People with heart conditions, high blood pressure, pregnancy, or caffeine sensitivity should limit caffeine and follow their clinician's advice.

quickGlance.situation: Your group is short on sleep and people still have to make decisions and do risky jobs.
immediate: Pull anyone showing drowsiness signs off driving, flames, medical care, or solo watch.
Set a written rest and watch rotation so someone is always awake and everyone gets sleep.
Use 15-30 minute naps with an alarm when real sleep is not possible.
then: Use caffeine only for critical windows and stop about 5 hours before sleep.
Protect sleep for the main decision-maker and anyone doing medical work.
Plan two good nights of recovery and avoid big decisions until then.

title: Resolving Conflict Inside a Group Under Stress
summary: A step-by-step way to settle arguments over chores, space, supplies, and decisions in a stressed household or group before they split it apart.

steps.title: Cool things down first
steps.body: No one solves a problem while shouting. If voices are rising, call a pause: 'Let's take ten minutes and come back to this.' Separate the people if needed and give each one something to drink or a quiet task. Check the basics - hunger, thirst, exhaustion, cold, and pain make every conflict worse, and many arguments disappear after food and sleep. The VA National Center for PTSD notes that anger and irritability are very common after disasters and suggests taking a break before a tense conversation. If anyone is threatening violence or has a weapon, stop here and focus on safety and de-escalation (see sec-009).

steps.title: Pick the right time, place, and helper
steps.body: Deal with the conflict soon - CERT leadership training says to resolve conflicts quickly and respectfully, because problems left alone grow. Choose a time when people are fed and rested and a place with some privacy. Avoid settling it in front of the whole group, which makes people defend their pride. If the leader is one of the people in the dispute, ask a neutral, trusted person to run the conversation instead. The helper's job is not to decide who is right; it is to keep the talk fair and moving.

steps.title: Set simple ground rules
steps.body: Start by agreeing on how you will talk. Keep it short: one person speaks at a time; no insults or name-calling; talk about the problem, not the person's character; and everyone is here to find something that works for the group. Federal mediators use this same idea in interest-based negotiation: the sides agree on ground rules and a shared goal before getting into the issues. Then state the shared goal out loud, for example: 'We all want to get through this winter without running out of firewood.'

steps.title: Listen until each side feels heard
steps.body: Let each person explain their view without interruption. Then have the other person, or the helper, repeat it back in their own words: 'So you're saying you've done the water runs four days in a row and no one noticed.' Ask, 'Did I get that right?' CERT training calls this empathetic listening: try to see the other person's view, listen for meaning, and paraphrase to confirm. People often calm down sharply once they feel understood, even before anything is solved. Watch tone of voice and body language too, not just words.

steps.title: Look for the need behind the demand
steps.body: A position is what someone says they want ('I want the back bedroom'). An interest is why ('I can't sleep with the baby crying, and I have the 2 a.m. watch'). Interest-based negotiation focuses on interests because there are usually several ways to meet them. Ask 'Why does that matter to you?' and 'What are you worried will happen?' Write the interests down. Often both sides share more than they think - both want rest, safety, or fairness - and the real fight is just about the method.

steps.title: Brainstorm options, then judge them fairly
steps.body: List every possible fix without judging any yet: swap watches, rotate the room weekly, hang a blanket as a sound barrier, move the baby's bed. Then agree on what makes a solution fair - for example, safe, doable with what we have, and equal in workload. Check each option against those standards, not against who argued louder. Federal mediators use this order: generate options first, agree on standards second, evaluate third. Combine pieces from different ideas if that works better. If something can't be settled now, 'park' it and set a time to come back to it.

steps.title: Agree, write it down, and check back
steps.body: State the agreement in plain words and confirm that each person accepts it. Write it down if it involves chores, supplies, or schedules, and post it where everyone can see. Set a check-in: 'Let's see how this works for three days.' If the agreement fails, return to the interests rather than the old positions. If two people truly cannot agree and a group decision is needed, the leader or the group decides by the agreed process, explains why, and expects everyone to follow it - disagreement is allowed, refusing to cooperate on safety is not.

steps.title: Prevent the next fight
steps.body: Most group conflict in emergencies comes from a few causes: unfair workload, unclear rules about supplies, lack of privacy, and decisions made without explanation. Fix these up front. Post a chore rotation. Set written rules for food, water, and fuel (see psych-009). Give each person a small private space, even just a corner and a bag. Explain the reason behind decisions in one sentence. Hold a short daily meeting where problems can be raised early, before they boil over.

warnings: If a conflict involves threats, weapons, or violence, stop mediating. Separate people, protect the vulnerable, and get help from authorities if possible.
Don't try to settle a dispute while people are exhausted, hungry, drunk, or furious. Wait until basics are handled.
Avoid public shaming. It hardens positions and can turn a small dispute into a lasting grudge.
Domestic violence or abuse is not a 'conflict' to mediate. Help the person at risk get to safety and contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) or 911.
proTips: Ask each side to restate the other's view before arguing their own. It cools tempers fast.
Use 'I' statements: 'I'm worried we'll run out' instead of 'You're wasting everything.'
Keep a written list of agreements so no one has to rely on memory.
A neutral helper with a simple script works better than a leader picking a winner.
source: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service / FEMA CERT / VA National Center for PTSD

sources.title: Steps in Interest-Based Negotiation
sources.publisher: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (via Air University Air Force Negotiation Center)

whenNotTo: During an immediate life-safety emergency - decide fast and sort out disagreements later.
When there is abuse, threats, or a weapon involved - focus on safety, not mediation.

quickGlance.situation: Two people or factions in your group are fighting over chores, space, supplies, or decisions.
immediate: Call a pause and separate people if voices are rising.
Check for hunger, thirst, and exhaustion before talking it out.
Agree on ground rules: one speaker at a time, no insults.
then: Have each side restate the other's view, then find the needs behind the demands.
Brainstorm options, judge them by agreed fairness standards, and write down the deal.
Set a check-in date to see if the agreement is working.

title: Mutual Aid and Organizing Your Neighborhood
summary: How to turn a street or building into a neighborhood that checks on each other, shares skills and tools, and works with official responders - starting before a disaster hits.

steps.title: Start small, before anything happens
steps.body: In most disasters, the first help people get comes from neighbors, not from professional responders. You don't need a formal group to start. Pick a manageable area - your block, one floor of an apartment building, or 10 to 20 homes. Knock on doors or leave a short note inviting people to a 30-minute meeting about getting ready for outages and storms. Keep it practical and friendly. Meet at a porch, driveway, community room, or place of worship. Your first goal is simply that neighbors know each other's names and faces, which makes checking on each other natural when the power goes out.

steps.title: Map people, skills, and needs
steps.body: With permission, make a simple contact list: names, addresses, phone numbers, and an out-of-area contact for each household. Ask who has useful skills - nursing, EMT, electrician, plumber, ham radio, carpentry, languages, childcare. Ask who may need extra help: older adults living alone, people with disabilities, people who rely on powered medical equipment or refrigerated medicine, families with infants, and people without a car. Let people share only what they are comfortable sharing. Keep the list private and on paper as well as on phones, since phones may die. Share it only with the people who need it.

steps.title: Inventory shared tools and supplies
steps.body: List equipment that could help the whole street: generators, chainsaws, ladders, wheelbarrows, a pickup truck, extra coolers, a camp stove, radios, first aid kits, solar chargers, and wet-dry vacuums. Note who owns each item and whether they are willing to lend it. Agree on simple rules: the owner decides how their item is used, borrowed items come back clean and fueled, and dangerous tools are only run by people trained to use them. Never run a generator or fuel-burning heater indoors or in a garage - carbon monoxide kills.

steps.title: Agree on a check-in plan and meeting point
steps.body: Decide how neighbors will check on each other after a storm, quake, or long outage. Assign each person or household a few nearby homes to check, with priority on those who may need help. Choose a meeting point that is safe and easy to find, plus a backup. Set a signal for homes that are okay versus need help - for example, a green or red card in the front window. Agree on how you will talk if phones are down: walking messengers, FRS or GMRS radios on a set channel, or a bulletin board at the meeting point. See comms-005 for family communication plans.

steps.title: Organize lightly when it happens
steps.body: After a disaster, use a simple structure modeled on CERT teams: one coordinator at the meeting point who tracks information, small teams of two or more people who go out to check homes, and someone keeping a written log of who needs what. Work in pairs; no one goes into damaged buildings alone. CERT training covers basic fire safety, light search and rescue, team organization, and disaster medical operations - but untrained neighbors should stick to checking on people, sharing supplies, and passing information. Report serious injuries, fires, gas leaks, and downed lines to 911 or official responders, and follow their directions when they arrive.

steps.title: Share fairly and protect dignity
steps.body: Mutual aid works because it is two-way: people give what they can and take what they need, without anyone being made to feel like a charity case. Set up shared resources in a calm, orderly way - a sign-up sheet for generator charging time, a shared cooler for medicines, a list for water runs. Prioritize those with medical needs, infants, and older adults. Keep records simple and transparent so no one suspects favoritism. Be careful about announcing large personal stockpiles widely; share within the trusted group (see sec-006 on keeping supplies private).

steps.title: Get trained and connect with official programs
steps.body: FEMA's Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) program has more than 3,200 local programs nationwide. Basic training teaches volunteers fire safety, light search and rescue, team organization, and disaster medical operations. FEMA's free online course IS-317, Introduction to CERT, is a good first step; contact your city or county emergency management office to find a local program. Ready.gov also encourages volunteering through reputable organizations listed by National Voluntary Organizations Active in Disaster (NVOAD), and notes that after a disaster, cash donations to reputable nonprofits usually help more than donated goods.

steps.title: Keep it alive with practice
steps.body: A plan that is never used is forgotten. Meet once or twice a year, update the contact list, and run a short drill - for example, everyone puts their window card up and the check teams do a 20-minute walk. Try a potluck during a planned power outage drill to test cooking and lighting. Each practice reveals gaps: a dead radio, a missing phone number, a neighbor who moved. Fix them and keep going. Neighborhood watch groups can build on this same network for night safety (see sec-012).

warnings: Untrained volunteers should not enter damaged or collapsed buildings, fight large fires, or handle downed power lines. Call 911 and wait for professionals.
Never run generators, grills, or fuel heaters indoors or in garages - carbon monoxide is a leading cause of death after storms.
Protect private information. Contact and medical-needs lists should be kept by a few trusted people only.
Be wary of people who suddenly show up offering paid 'help' or asking for personal information after a disaster - scams are common (see sec-008).
proTips: Pair each person who needs help with two neighbors, so there is always a backup.
Print the contact list and map; laminate one copy for the meeting point.
Agree on one FRS or GMRS channel for the neighborhood ahead of time.
FEMA's IS-317 course is free and online - a great first step for the organizer.
whenNotTo: When officials order an evacuation - leave; do not stay behind to run neighborhood operations.
When conditions are unsafe (active fire, flooding, gas leak) - get to safety first and organize afterward.

quickGlance.situation: You want your street or building to look after each other in emergencies.
immediate: Invite 10-20 nearby households to a short meeting.
Make a private contact list with skills and who may need extra help.
Pick a meeting point, a backup, and an okay/help window signal.
then: List shared tools and agree on lending rules.
Take FEMA's free IS-317 course and find a local CERT program.
Drill once or twice a year and update the list.

title: Running Your Household Like an Incident Command
summary: Borrow the basics of FEMA's Incident Command System - one person in charge, clear roles, short briefings, written task lists, and clean handoffs - to run your home smoothly through an outage or disaster.

steps.title: Name one person in charge
steps.body: In the Incident Command System (ICS) used by U.S. responders, every incident has one Incident Commander from the start. At home, pick one adult to coordinate - often whoever is calmest and has the most relevant knowledge, not necessarily the oldest. This person does not do everything; they keep the big picture, set priorities, and make final calls when the family can't agree. Name a backup too. ICS uses 'unity of command': each person takes assignments from only one supervisor. In a family that means kids are not getting three different instructions from three adults. Decide this ahead of time, and write it in your family emergency plan.

steps.title: Assign the four main roles
steps.body: ICS has four main sections, and they map well onto a household. Operations does the hands-on work: setting up lights, hauling water, cooking, caring for the sick. Planning tracks information: weather and news updates, how many days of water and fuel are left, and the written plan. Logistics finds and manages supplies: inventory, batteries, fuel, borrowing from neighbors. Finance and admin handles cash, receipts, insurance photos, and important documents. In a small family, one person may hold two or three roles. Give children real but safe pieces of these jobs, such as counting batteries or keeping the log.

steps.title: Set objectives for each period
steps.body: ICS uses 'management by objectives' and plans in 'operational periods' - blocks of time with clear goals. At home, use a morning-to-evening and evening-to-morning cycle. For each period, write 2 to 4 specific goals: 'Fill all water containers by noon.' 'Move freezer food to coolers.' 'Check on Mrs. Lee next door.' 'Charge all phones and radios from the car.' Specific goals with a deadline get done. Vague goals like 'stay safe' do not. Put life-safety items first, then problems about to get worse, then comfort.

steps.title: Hold short briefings
steps.body: Start each period with a 5 to 10 minute briefing, standing up. Cover: current situation (power status, weather, official alerts), what's left (water, food, fuel, medicine), today's objectives, who does what, safety reminders (no generators indoors, candles watched), and the next check-in time. Ask each person to say their task back. Keep it brief and calm - children absorb the tone. End-of-day check-ins cover what got done, what didn't, and any problems. ICS also stresses using plain language instead of jargon or codes, which matters even more at a kitchen table.

steps.title: Keep a written task board and log
steps.body: Write tasks on paper, a whiteboard, or a taped-up sheet: task, who owns it, when it's due, and a box to check when done. This is your household version of an Incident Action Plan. Keep a separate running log with the time and key events: 'Power out 6:10 p.m.' 'Boil-water notice 9:00 a.m.' 'Gave Dad his 8 a.m. meds.' A log helps the next person on shift, protects against tired memory, and is useful later for insurance claims. Track supplies on the same board so everyone can see how many days of water and fuel are left.

steps.title: Keep span of control small and check in and out
steps.body: ICS suggests one supervisor for about five people. In a larger household or multi-family group, split into small teams with a lead each, and the coordinator talks mainly to the leads. Use check-in and check-out: anyone leaving the house says where they are going, who they are with, and when they will be back, and reports when they return. Never send kids or anyone else out alone after dark or into damaged areas. If someone doesn't return on time, you'll know right away and can act (see security-004 for rally points and lost-person steps).

steps.title: Hand off cleanly
steps.body: ICS requires a briefing whenever command changes. When the coordinator needs to sleep, or another adult takes over a role, do a short handoff: what is happening now, what's in progress, what's planned, and any concerns. Point to the task board and log. Say clearly, 'You're in charge until 6 a.m.' The person taking over repeats the key points back. Clean handoffs prevent the classic failure where both adults think the other one turned off the stove or locked the door.

steps.title: Scale up, scale down, and debrief
steps.body: ICS is designed to expand or shrink with the size of the problem. A short outage might need only one coordinator and a task list. A week-long emergency might need every role filled and a neighbor or two folded in. When things return to normal, stand the structure down on purpose and say thank you. Then hold a 15-minute debrief: what worked, what didn't, what supplies ran out first, and what to fix in the plan. Update your kit and plan right away while lessons are fresh.

warnings: Don't let structure slow down a true emergency. If there's a fire, gas smell, or medical crisis, act first and organize afterward.
One coordinator does not mean one person does all the work - that leads to burnout and mistakes.
Check-in and check-out rules matter most after dark and in damaged areas. Never let anyone go out alone without a return time.
proTips: Laminate a one-page household ICS card: roles, briefing checklist, and task-board template.
Use a whiteboard and dry-erase markers; they work without power and everyone can see them.
Practice once during a planned 'lights out' evening so roles feel natural.
FEMA's free online IS-100.c course explains ICS in a few hours.
source: FEMA Emergency Management Institute IS-100.c (ICS) / FEMA CERT

sources.title: IS-100.c Introduction to the Incident Command System (class handouts)
sources.publisher: FEMA Emergency Management Institute (via URMC Finger Lakes Regional Training Center)

whenNotTo: In the first seconds of a fire, collapse, or medical emergency - act immediately and set up structure once people are safe.
For a very short outage - a quick plan and one person keeping track is enough.

quickGlance.situation: Your household faces an outage or disaster that will last more than a few hours.
immediate: Name one coordinator and a backup.
Assign roles: hands-on work, information tracking, supplies, and documents/cash.
Hold a 5-10 minute briefing and write 2-4 goals for this period.
then: Keep a task board, supply count, and time log.
Use check-in and check-out for anyone leaving the house.
Do a spoken handoff at every shift change and debrief when it's over.

title: Fair Rationing and Resource Decisions in a Group
summary: How a household or group can count what it has, set clear and fair rules for food, fuel, and medicine, protect the most vulnerable, and avoid the fights that scarcity causes. Includes the key safety rule: do not ration drinking water.

steps.title: Count everything first
steps.body: You can't share fairly what you haven't counted. Do a full inventory as early as possible: water in gallons, food in meals or rough calories, fuel, batteries, medicines (with expiration dates), and hygiene supplies. Have two people count together and write it down; this prevents both mistakes and suspicion. Then divide by the number of people to get 'days of supply.' For example, Ready.gov recommends one gallon of water per person per day for drinking and sanitation. If four people have 24 gallons, that is about 6 days. Post the totals where the group can see them and update them daily.

steps.title: Do not ration drinking water
steps.body: Health officials are clear on this point: never ration drinking water. If supplies are low, drink what you need today and work hard to find or make more for tomorrow. Dehydration causes confusion, poor decisions, and serious illness quickly. A normally active person needs at least about 2 quarts (about 2 liters) of drinking water a day, and heat can roughly double that. Children, nursing mothers, and sick people need even more. Cut water use elsewhere instead: limit washing, reuse gray water for flushing, and reduce physical activity and stay cool to lower how much your body needs. See water-015 and water-010.

steps.title: Ration food carefully - with exceptions
steps.body: Unlike water, food can be rationed safely for a while for most healthy adults. Health officials note that healthy people can get by on about half their usual food for an extended time. Do not cut food for children or pregnant women, and be careful with nursing mothers, older adults, people who are sick, and anyone with diabetes or other medical conditions - they may need regular meals or special foods. In an outage, eat food from the refrigerator first, then the freezer, and save shelf-stable food for last (see home-004 for food safety). Plan meals for the whole household in advance (see food-013) rather than letting people graze.

steps.title: Agree on the rules together, in advance
steps.body: Rules feel fair when people help make them and understand why. Hold a short meeting to agree on: daily portions, who gets priority, how medicines are handled, what counts as personal versus shared supplies, and how the rules will change if the situation gets better or worse. Write them down in plain words and post them. Use clear standards, such as medical need first, equal shares for healthy adults, and extra for those doing heavy work. Deciding the standards first, then applying them, is the same approach federal mediators use to settle disputes fairly.

steps.title: Protect the most vulnerable
steps.body: Set aside supplies for those who cannot go without: infant formula and baby food, prescription and critical medicines, food for people with diabetes or allergies, and extra water for children, nursing mothers, and the sick. Mark these supplies clearly and keep them separate. People who need refrigerated or powered medical equipment may need a larger share of fuel or battery power. Being open about why these people get priority prevents resentment. Most people accept unequal shares when the reason is clear and the same rules apply to everyone.

steps.title: Make sharing transparent
steps.body: Suspicion destroys groups faster than hunger. Have two people handle distribution, rotating the job. Serve meals at set times, together if possible, so everyone can see portions. Keep a simple log of what was used each day. Store shared supplies in one place with limited access, and lock or secure them if trust is low. Never let one person control all supplies without oversight - even an honest person will face accusations. If someone is caught taking extra, deal with it calmly and privately first, using the conflict steps in psych-006.

steps.title: Decide on fuel, power, and other limited resources
steps.body: Use the same process for fuel, batteries, and generator time. List what each resource is needed for, rank uses by importance, and set a budget. A typical order: medical devices and medicine storage, safe heating or cooling for vulnerable people, water purification, communication (radios and phones), food safety, then lighting and comfort. Post a schedule, for example, 'Generator runs 7-9 a.m. and 6-8 p.m.; medical devices charge first.' Never run generators or fuel heaters indoors.

steps.title: Review and adjust
steps.body: Check the inventory and the rules every day or two. If resupply arrives, loosen the rules and say so. If it's getting worse, tighten them early rather than late - small cuts now are easier than big ones later. Explain each change and the numbers behind it. Watch people for signs of not getting enough food or water: dizziness, confusion, very dark urine, weakness, or a child who is unusually sleepy or irritable. Treat these as warnings to adjust portions, and get medical help if they are severe.

warnings: Never ration drinking water. Drink what you need today and look for more for tomorrow.
Do not cut food for children or pregnant women. Be cautious with nursing mothers, older adults, sick people, and people with diabetes or other medical conditions.
Never let one person control all supplies with no oversight - it invites both abuse and false accusations.
Do not ration prescription medicines by skipping or splitting doses without talking to a pharmacist or doctor.
proTips: Count supplies with two people and post the totals and 'days left' on a board.
Serve meals at set times so everyone sees the portions.
Keep a separate, clearly marked kit for babies, medicines, and special diets.
Decide the rules before you're hungry - people are far more reasonable on a full stomach.
source: Ready.gov (FEMA) / Mississippi State Department of Health

sources.title: Steps in Interest-Based Negotiation
sources.publisher: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (via Air University Air Force Negotiation Center)

whenNotTo: Do not apply food cuts to children, pregnant women, or people with medical conditions that need regular meals.
Do not ration water - reduce other uses of water instead.

quickGlance.situation: Your household or group has limited food, water, fuel, or medicine and no resupply in sight.
immediate: Count all supplies with two people and figure days left per person.
Do not ration drinking water - cut other water uses instead.
Set aside supplies for babies, medicines, and medical needs.
then: Agree on written rules and post them.
Serve meals at set times and log what is used.
Review the numbers every day or two and adjust early.
